description: Running project scripts with npm run, and one-off tools with npx.

screens.body:
The scripts field in package.json maps short names to terminal commands. It's your project's remote control.

Instead of remembering node --watch --experimental-strip-types src/app.js, you just write it once and give it a name.

Team members then run the same command the same way — no more "works on my machine" because someone typed the command differently.

options: They're short, saved commands from package.json
They're JavaScript functions in your code
check.question: What is the scripts field?

screens.heading: The scripts field

screens.body:
npm run <name> executes the command saved under that name. npm run dev, npm run build, npm run whatever-you-named-it.

The command runs with your project's node_modules/.bin on the PATH, so locally installed tools (like jest or esbuild) just work.

That last bit is quietly magical: no global installs needed for your project's tools.

check.question: package.json has "dev": "node --watch src/app.js". How do you run it?

code.snippet:
$ npm run dev
> my-app@1.0.0 dev
> node --watch src/app.js
# restarts automatically every time you save

screens.heading: npm run
screens.keyPoint: npm run <name> runs the saved command.

screens.body:
Two script names are VIPs: start and test. They get shortcuts — npm start and npm test, no run needed.

npm start conventionally launches your app in production mode. npm test runs your test suite.

Any other name still needs npm run: npm run lint, npm run format, npm run deploy.

check.question: Which scripts can you run without the word "run"?

code.snippet:
$ npm start     # shortcut for: npm run start
$ npm test      # shortcut for: npm run test
$ npm run lint  # everything else still needs "run"

screens.heading: start and test: the VIP scripts
screens.keyPoint: npm start and npm test skip the word run.

screens.body:
Scripts sometimes need arguments — like which file to lint. npm passes them through, but you need a separator.

Put -- between the script name and your arguments. Everything after -- goes to your command, not to npm.

Without the --, npm tries to interpret your arguments as its own flags, and chaos follows.

check.question: Your greet script takes a --name flag. How do you pass it?

code.snippet:
$ npm run greet -- --name Roli
# the script receives: --name Roli

screens.heading: Passing arguments
screens.keyPoint: -- separates npm's args from your script's args.

screens.body:
npx runs a package's tool without installing it first. One command, zero commitment.

npx cowsay "hello" fetches cowsay, runs it, and cleans up. Your project stays untouched.

It's perfect for one-off tools and scaffolders — the things you run once and never think about again.

options: Run a package's tool without installing it
check.question: What does npx do?

screens.heading: What is npx?
screens.keyPoint: npx = try a tool without installing it.

screens.body:
The old way to use CLI tools was npm install -g: one global copy for your whole computer. The problem? Every project wanted a different version.

npx skips that mess. It uses the version in your project if there is one, or grabs a fresh copy temporarily.

Rule of thumb: tools your project depends on go in devDependencies and run via npm run. One-off tools go through npx.

options: npx uses the project's version or fetches a fresh one — no version fights
check.question: Why prefer npx over npm install -g for CLI tools?

code.snippet:
$ npx create-vite my-app   # scaffold a project, nothing installed globally
$ npx prettier --write .   # one-off format, then it's gone

screens.heading: npx vs global installs
screens.keyPoint: npx avoids global version fights. Use it for one-offs.

screens.body:
Most projects end up with the same handful of scripts. Here's the classic trio:

dev: run locally with auto-restart while you code. build: bundle everything into a dist/ folder. start: launch the built app.

A new developer clones the repo, runs npm install, then npm run dev — and they're coding in minutes. That's the dream.

check.question: Name the classic three scripts for a web project.

screens.heading: A typical script pipeline
screens.keyPoint: dev → build → start: the lifecycle of most projects.
